Exercises STAT340 - ANOVA - part II

  • 1 Ex-2: Yield of barley
  • 2 Ex-2: Indicator variable (ANCOVA model)





Colloquium exercises: You are encouraged to work together in groups on the exercises. Sharing problems and solutions is often a much quicker way to learn, especially for problems of a more practical nature.

Here are some packages and data you need to use in these exercises. So you should run these commands before you start the exercises.

library(mixlm)
library(car)
library(effects)
library(BIAS.data)
data(NSRdata)
data(Barley)
data(birth)

1 Ex-2: Yield of barley

In Barley there are results from an experiment where the response is yield of barley pr 1000 square meter, and the factors varieties of barley, soil types, types of fertilizers. In addition was the experiment done in two different geographical areas (sites).

  • Assume a two factor model including the main effects of Variety and Soil and their interaction. State the model and explain all parameters under a sum-to-zero parametrization.
Solution

The model can be written as: \[ y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + (\alpha\beta)_{ij} + \epsilon_{ijk}\] where, \(\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\)

The parametrization restrictions for “sum-to-zero”” are: \[ \begin{eqnarray} \sum_i{\alpha_i} = 0, & \sum_j{\beta_j} = 0, & \sum_{i}{(\alpha\beta)_{ij}} = 0 \text{ and } \sum_{j}{(\alpha\beta)_{ij}} = 0 \end{eqnarray} \]

  • Fit the model in R and estimate all parameters
Solution 
# either
mod1 <- mixlm::lm(Yield ~ Variety * Soil, data = Barley, contrasts="contr.sum")
# or
mod1 <- stats::lm(Yield ~ Variety * Soil, data = Barley, contrasts = list(x = contr.sum))
## Warning in model.matrix.default(mt, mf, contrasts): variable 'x' is absent, its
## contrast will be ignored
summod1 <- summary(mod1, cor=FALSE)
print(summod1)
## 
## Call:
## stats::lm(formula = Yield ~ Variety * Soil, data = Barley, contrasts = list(x = contr.sum))
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -88.469 -44.322   5.009  35.219 106.913 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                    Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)          385.17      19.30  19.955   <2e-16 ***
## VarietyC2             56.96      27.30   2.087   0.0462 *  
## SoilSand             -35.71      27.30  -1.308   0.2015    
## VarietyC2:SoilSand   -73.62      38.60  -1.907   0.0668 .  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 54.6 on 28 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.4022, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3382 
## F-statistic:  6.28 on 3 and 28 DF,  p-value: 0.002142
anova(mod1)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: Yield
##              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
## Variety       1   3247    3247  1.0893 0.3055521    
## Soil          1  42071   42071 14.1146 0.0008031 ***
## Variety:Soil  1  10841   10841  3.6370 0.0668166 .  
## Residuals    28  83459    2981                      
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

From the model summaries we find the estimated parameters to be:

  1. The estimated overall mean yield: \(\hat{\mu}=\) 385.1745876
  2. The estimated effects of Variety 1 and 2: \(\hat{\alpha}_1=\) 56.9574066, \(\hat{\alpha}_2 = -\hat{\alpha}_1 =\) -56.9574066
  3. The estimated effects of Soil 1 and 2: \(\hat{\beta}_1=\) -35.7065893, \(\hat{\beta}_2 = -\hat{\beta}_1 =\) 35.7065893
  4. The estimated interaction effects of Variety and Soil: \(\hat{\alpha\beta}_{11}=\) -73.62293, \(\hat{\alpha\beta}_{12}=-\hat{\alpha\beta}_{11}=\) 73.62293, \(\hat{\alpha\beta}_{21}=-\hat{\alpha\beta}_{11}=\) 73.62293, \(\hat{\alpha\beta}_{22}=-\hat{\alpha\beta}_{21}=-\hat{\alpha\beta}_{12}=\) -73.62293
  5. The estimated within variety:Soil levels unexplained variability: \(\hat{\sigma}^2=MSE=\) 2980.67
  • Make an interaction plot and try to conclude about the presence of interaction from the plot. How would you explain interaction effect in this example for a person with experience in agriculture, but minimal statistical experience?
Solution 
plot(allEffects(mod1,confidence.level = .95))

From the plot, it seems that a farmer can expect an increase in yield when using Variety 2 instead of Variety 1 for Soil = Clay, but vice versa for Soil = Sand. If this is so, there is a so-called interaction effect of Variety and Soil on yield.

  • Perform a hypothesis test for the interaction effect. Conclusion?
Solution 
anova(mod1)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Response: Yield
##              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
## Variety       1   3247    3247  1.0893 0.3055521    
## Soil          1  42071   42071 14.1146 0.0008031 ***
## Variety:Soil  1  10841   10841  3.6370 0.0668166 .  
## Residuals    28  83459    2981                      
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The interaction between Soil and Variety is insignificant at 5% testlevel (p-value > 0.05). This result indicates that the slight non-parallel tendency of the lines in the interaction plot may be due to random errors. More data would be needed to verify any interaction effect.

  • Fit a four factor model with Variety, Soil, Fetilizer and Site as factors and with all possible 2-factor, 3-factor and 4-factor interactions. Are there any higher order significant effects? Compare the R-squared and the adjusted R-squared values. What can you conclude from these?

There is only one main effect and one interaction effect significant at 5% levels, namely the Fertilizer main effect and the Soil:Fertilizer interaction. However, the least squares estimator is prone to inflated variance estimates and difficulties in finding significance when the number of variables k rises compared to the number of observations N and if variables are highly correlated. Too many variables to estimate from a limited number of observations leaves few degrees of freedom to SSE, and tests with low power. Lack of significance may be an over-fitting problem. By removing some of the least significant variables, the problem is reduced, and a reduced model with significant effects may be identified.

The large difference between \(R^2\) and \(R_{adj}^2\) is also an indication of an over-fitted model.

  • Try to reduce the model by excluding the least significant higher order interactions first, one at a time, in a backward elimination procedure using the ‘backward’ function from the mixlm package. Use the ‘hierarchy = TRUE’ argument to ensure that the so-called marginality principle is followed. What is the final reduced model?
Solution 
mod2.red <- backward(mod2, alpha = 0.05, full = TRUE, hierarchy = TRUE)
## Backward elimination, alpha-to-remove: 0.05

##     Variety:Soil:Fertilizer + Variety:Soil:Site + Variety:Fertilizer:Site + 
##     Soil:Fertilizer:Site + Variety:Soil:Fertilizer:Site

anova(mod2.red)
## Analysis of Variance Table

## Fertilizer               1   9846    9846 17.9732 0.0004019 ***

## Soil:Site                1   1405    1405  2.5642 0.1249852    
## Variety:Soil:Fertilizer  1   3639    3639  6.6432 0.0179818 *  
## Variety:Soil:Site        1   2671    2671  4.8752 0.0390875 *  
## Residuals               20  10956     548                      
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The final reduced model is a model with all four main effects, three of which are now significant, five 2-order interactions (three significant), and two significant 3-order interactions. The 4-order interaction is removed. The marginality principle says that we should keep all main effects and interactions that are part of higher order significant interaction(s) in the model. This is a good principle for practical data analysis.

  • Perform a model check of the reduced model using residual analysis.
Solution

The backward function has fitted the reduced model:

par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(mod2.red, which = c(1,2,4,5))

The residual plots give no evidence of any problems with the model assumptions.

  • You can make the third order interaction effects plot between Variety,Site and Soil like this:
eff <- allEffects(mod2.red, confidence.level = .95)
plot(eff[2])

Try to explain the plot. Why do you think the interaction between Variety,Site and Soil was significant?

Solution

The interaction effect is significant because the lines are not parallel. The effect of Soil on Yield is different for the two Varieties and the effect of Soil on Yield for one Variety may depend on Site. This is a three-way interaction effect.

2 Ex-2: Indicator variable (ANCOVA model)

This exercise is a follow up on the exercise from week 3 on multiple regression using the mtcars data set.

  • The am variable is really an indicator variable for transmission system of the cars (The variable is coded as 0=automatic, 1=manual). Fit a multiple linear model with “cyl”, “wt”, “am” and the interaction between “wt” and “am” and report the summary of the model with parameter estimates and tests.

NOTE: Make sure the am is treated as a categorical variable in the model by writing factor(am) in the model formula in the linear model function. Use the default “sum to zero” parametrization when you fit the model.

Solution 
cars <- lm(mpg ~ cyl + wt * factor(am), data=mtcars, contrasts="contr.sum")
summary(cars)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = mpg ~ cyl + wt * factor(am), data = mtcars, contrasts = "contr.sum")
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -3.4621 -1.4913 -0.7879  1.3959  5.3499 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)       40.2523     1.9170  20.997  < 2e-16 ***
## cyl               -1.1814     0.3803  -3.106  0.00442 ** 
## wt                -4.4676     0.8943  -4.996 3.08e-05 ***
## factor(am)(0)     -5.9693     1.9227  -3.105  0.00444 ** 
## wt:factor(am)(0)   2.0987     0.6558   3.200  0.00350 ** 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## s: 2.265 on 27 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared: 0.877,
## Adjusted R-squared: 0.8588 
## F-statistic: 48.13 on 4 and 27 DF,  p-value: 6.643e-12
  • Write up the assumed model which has been run here. Also write up the estimated models for automatic and manual transmission, respectively.
Solution

The model is:

\[ y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \beta_4 x_2\cdot x_3 + \epsilon \]

where \(y\)=mpg, \(x_1\)=cyl, \(x_2\)=wt, \(x_3\)=am and \(\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\).

For automatic transmission (am=\(x_3\)=1) we have the estimated model: \[ \begin{split} \hat{y} &= 40.2523 - 1.1814x_1 - 4.4676x_2 - 5.9693 + 2.0987x_2\\ &=34.283 - 1.1814x_1 - 2.3689x_2 \end{split} \]

For manual transmission (am=\(x_3\)=-1) we have \[ \begin{split} \hat{y} &= 40.2523 - 1.1814x_1 - 4.4676x_2 + 5.9693 - 2.0987x_2\\ &= 46.2216 - 1.1814x_1 - 6.5663x_2 \end{split} \]

We observe that the negative effect of weight on mileage is larger for manual transmission than for automatic.
